# Meaning as Region: Concepts, Hierarchies and Subspaces {#sec-ch-meaning-as-region}

<!-- Task 6 template -->
*Part I, the Librarian Test: can a computer shelve and find things by meaning alone, with one fixed place for each thing?* This chapter follows @sec-ch-meaning-as-direction. **Question: does a region hold a concept better than a point?**

*Data, models and loss.* Data: The text8 SGNS space and the WordNet hypernym tree, for the Poincare embedding of nouns. The models are in @sec-ch-zoo-of-models; the loss of each is stated there once.

| Model | Zoo | Role in this chapter |
|:--|:--|:--|
| SGNS | @sec-zoo-sgns | points, the baseline |
| Poincare | @sec-zoo-poincare | a hierarchy in curved space |

A concept is a region and not a point. A point says where one thing is; the meaning of a word such as "dog" covers many things, some more typical than others, with a boundary that is blurred and members that are held by overlapping resemblances and not by one shared feature. Rosch found that categories have graded membership and a best example [@rosch1975cognitive]; Gärdenfors proposed that concepts are convex regions of quality spaces [@gardenfors2000conceptual]; Wittgenstein's family resemblance says that a family is a connected set and not a ball [@wittgenstein1953philosophical]. The question of this chapter is what shape a concept has in a trained space (a ball, a box, a cone, a subspace, a region of a curved space) and whether any of these beats a point of the same size on a stated judge.

The scope is the extent and the structure of concepts: typicality, hierarchy (a dog is a mammal) and negation as complement. It does not cover the likeness of two points (@sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness), a single quality (@sec-ch-meaning-as-direction), a concept that moves or changes (the chapter on generation of the chapter on generation, @sec-prop-paths), or the composition of two concepts into a third (@sec-ch-meaning-and-structure).

*Goals and expectations (proposed, to be confirmed by the author before any experiment).*

*Goal 1, prototypes and graded membership (Rosch).* The expectation is that the cosine of a word to the centroid of its category correlates with human typicality ratings, against a shuffled-label null. The run needs a typicality norm (Rosch's own, or a later one); the data are to be specified (@sec-reg-prototypes).

*Goal 2, convexity (Gärdenfors).* The expectation is that the members of a category lie in a region that excludes non-members more than a random set of the same size does; the convex hull in a high-dimensional space contains almost everything, so the test must use a low-dimensional subspace or a linear separator. The categories and the test are to be specified (@sec-reg-convex). *This goal receives Q17 (@sec-likeness-handed-to-meaning-as-region).*

*Goal 3, hierarchy as containment (Vilnis, Nickel, Tifrea).* The expectation, from the theory, is that a tree embeds with low distortion in a hyperbolic space of a few dimensions and with high distortion in a Euclidean space of the same dimension, and that boxes represent entailment as containment. The run embeds a small tree in both spaces and measures the distortion, which has an analytic answer to check against (@sec-hyperbolic-spaces).

*Goal 4, a tree in the geometry (Hewitt and Manning).* The expectation is that the distances between words in the syntax tree of a sentence are recoverable by a linear map from the contextual vectors of a model better than from static vectors. The run is the structural probe, with its control task (@sec-tree-geometry).

*Goal 5, negation as complement (Birkhoff and von Neumann, Widdows).* If a concept is a subspace, its negation is the orthogonal complement and exclusion is orthogonality. The run is the toy of the chapter on difference, here applied to concepts as subspaces (@sec-concepts-subspaces).

## What the Philosophies Say About Regions {#sec-reg-philosophy}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Rosch on prototypes and the best example [@rosch1975cognitive]; Gärdenfors on convex regions [@gardenfors2000conceptual]; Wittgenstein on family resemblance and on boundaries drawn for a purpose [@wittgenstein1953philosophical, §§66–71]; Goodman's three discs, alike in pairs with no feature common to all three [@goodman1972seven]; Putnam on extension and intension [@putnam1975meaning]; and the logic of subspaces [@birkhoff1936logic]. For each: what shape of region it implies (a ball around a prototype, a convex set, a connected set held by chains, a subspace), and where a vector stops: a region has a boundary and a size, and a point has neither.*

## Typicality and Prototypes {#sec-reg-prototypes}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Goal 1. The cosine to the centroid and to the nearest member, against typicality; the effect of the raw cosine's artefacts (frequency, a common direction) from the chapter on likeness. Null: shuffled ratings; judge: a typicality norm.*

## Are Categories Convex? {#sec-reg-convex}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Goal 2. A linear separator of a category against the rest, its accuracy on held-out words, and the same for random categories of the same size; the share of non-members inside the convex hull of the members in a low-dimensional projection. The chain test of the chapter on likeness (neighbours of neighbours) is the family-resemblance counterpart: a concept held by chains is connected and not convex.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/meaning_as_likeness.qmd, section sec-likeness-other-objects -->
## Changing the Object Changes the Likeness {#sec-likeness-other-objects}

*Plan (1 page, a table and three short paragraphs; the section only states which likeness each representation defines, and the models are taken up in the chapters named, so nothing here is measured). The last section asked whether likeness is a distance. This one asks what happens when the object is not a point. The distributional hypothesis [@harris1954distributional; @firth1957synopsis] says that words in similar contexts are alike, and a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a cosine or a Euclidean distance turns that into proximity. Proximity brings the metric axioms, and the previous section showed that judged likeness breaks them. Each alternative below keeps the distributional idea and changes the object that is learned, or the score that compares two objects, so that one axiom is given up on purpose. The reading is the author's, from a discussion, and each claim of a source is to be read before it is kept.*

| Object and score | What "alike" becomes | Axiom given up | What it is meant to carry | Chapter |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Point, cosine or Euclidean | Small angle or distance | None (the baseline) | Topical association, symmetric synonymy | here |
| Point in hyperbolic space, geodesic distance [@nickel2017poincare] | A short path, which passes near a common ancestor | Flatness: volume grows exponentially with the radius, so a tree fits in few dimensions | Taxonomy, with the norm read as level of generality | @sec-hyperbolic-spaces |
| Box, volume of intersection [@vilnis2018probabilistic] | $\mathrm{Vol}(A \cap B) / \mathrm{Vol}(B)$, read as $P(A \mid B)$ | Symmetry | Entailment: "dog" is inside "mammal", not near it | @sec-hyperbolic-spaces |
| Gaussian, divergence [@vilnis2015word] | Overlap of two densities | A point's lack of width; symmetry too, if the divergence is KL | Breadth, so a polysemous or general word has a large covariance | @sec-hyperbolic-spaces |
| Sparse code, shared active features [@bricken2023towards] | Overlap of the sets of active features | Dense, rotation-free coordinates | Alike if the same features fire | @sec-features-directions |
| Set of token vectors, MaxSim [@khattab2020colbert] | $\sum_i \max_j \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{d}_j$, an alignment | Symmetry, and one vector per item | Every constraint of the query found in the document | @sec-hybrid-search-multi-vector |
| Structural alignment of parts (Gentner 1983 [@gentner1983structure]; [@medin1993respects]) | Similarity is a one-to-one, relationally consistent mapping of the parts of two things, and matches that belong to a larger system count for more | Symmetry, additivity and one score per pair | Respect fixed by the comparison, and inferences carried from one thing to the other | @sec-likeness-phrases-sentences |
| Entity, relation as a rotation in $\mathbb{C}^d$ [@sun2019rotate] | Two pairs are alike if one operator maps both | The relation of likeness between the two ends of a pair | Typed relations: Paris and France are not alike, and are related by *capital of* | @sec-ch-meaning-as-difference |

*Three points of care, since the discussion put them in a strong form. (1) Distinct objects do not each give a better likeness; they give a different one. A box and a hyperbolic point both encode hierarchy, but a box answers "is $A$ inside $B$" and a point answers "how far up the tree is it", and which is better is a question for a hierarchy benchmark, not for this chapter. The hyperbolic norm as generality is a claim for a model trained on a tree; whether a space trained on text puts "entity" near the origin is the test of @sec-tree-geometry. (2) The Gaussian row needs the divergence named: KL is asymmetric and Wasserstein is symmetric, so "Gaussians break symmetry" holds for one and not for the other. (3) The sparse-code row says that two inputs are alike when they use the same features, which is a claim about a dictionary; whether the features are circuits of the model is a different claim, and the section does not make it.*

*What the four sources read for this table say (PDFs; the first is a web article saved as a PDF, 97 pages). Vilnis et al. (2018) embed concepts as boxes (hyperrectangles) whose volumes are probabilities, so that an asymmetric, transitive relation such as entailment or hypernymy is containment and the conditional probability is the fraction of one box inside the other, with results on WordNet hypernymy and on Flickr entailment; they present it as a probabilistic extension of order embeddings, with a better treatment of uncertainty (the claim of the table, that "dog" is inside "mammal", is the design purpose of the model and not a result about text corpora). Khattab and Zaharia (2020) compute the relevance of a document to a query as the sum over the query tokens of the maximum similarity to any document token (MaxSim, "late interaction"), with the two sides encoded independently so that document vectors can be stored, which is the cheap approximation to the alignment of Medin, Goldstone and Gentner and the reason it is asymmetric. Bricken et al. (2023, *Transformer Circuits Thread*) train sparse autoencoders on the 512-neuron MLP activations of a one-layer transformer (8 billion data points, dictionaries from 512 to 131,072 features, detailed analysis on 4,096) and report that the features are more interpretable than the neurons (a blinded annotator, one of the authors, scoring 412 activation intervals of 162 features and neurons on a rubric: median feature 12, median neuron 0), that of the 4,096 features 168 are dead and 292 of ultralow density, and, for universality, that a feature of one run has a closest feature in a run of another transformer, with other seeds, whose activations correlate at a median of 0.72, against 0.46 for the closest neuron. Two cautions for this row. The "closest feature" is chosen by a maximum over 4,096 candidates, which inflates the median, and the comparison is of two one-layer models; and *feature splitting* (a single feature of a small dictionary, such as a base64 feature, splits into several finer ones as the dictionary grows, with a graph that "may both split and merge" and is not a tree) means that "same active features" depends on the size of the dictionary, so a likeness read as overlap of features is relative to a resolution, which is Goodman's relativity in a new place. Sun et al. (2019) define a relation as a rotation of the head entity vector into the tail in complex space and show that this can express symmetry and antisymmetry, inversion and composition of relations, which a translation cannot; the relation of two entities is then the existence of a relation-specific operator and not a small distance.*

*What the table does not support, and the section says so. The summary "the field has moved from one scalar likeness to separate geometric properties for topic (angle), generality (norm or volume), ambiguity (variance) and analogy (operator)" is a hypothesis about the direction of the field, and in practice a cosine on a dense vector is still the default of retrieval and of evaluation. The claim to keep is the weaker one: a likeness is defined by an object together with a score, so the question "are these two alike" has no answer until both are given. A test the book can run is the one this chapter uses everywhere: the same pairs, the same judge, and the ordering of the representations by the likeness each is credited with.*

## Concepts as Subspaces {#sec-concepts-subspaces}
*The logic of subspaces (Birkhoff and von Neumann): negation as orthogonal complement, and why that logic is not distributive. A concept such as "dog" is better described as a subspace, with directions shared by all modalities and directions specific to each, than as a single point. This section does not need complex numbers: the construction works over the reals, and the chapter says so. In this logic, containment of subspaces is implication, orthogonality is exclusion, and anything else is undetermined, which is the geometric reading of "entailed, refuted, undetermined" tested in @sec-ch-meaning-and-truth.*

Sources (first pass). The logic of subspaces [@birkhoff1936logic]; negation and disjunction in vector-space retrieval and semantics [@widdows2004geometry].

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/tangent_spaces_geodesics.qmd, section sec-hyperbolic-spaces -->
## Hyperbolic Latent Spaces {#sec-hyperbolic-spaces}
*Why negative curvature suits trees (volume grows exponentially with radius), and the Poincaré ball and Lorentz hyperboloid models for embedding trees and hierarchical taxonomies with arbitrarily low distortion in few dimensions, against the dimension cost of doing the same in flat space.*

*Hierarchy has other encodings, compared by the likeness each defines in @sec-likeness-other-objects: box embeddings, where "dog" is inside "mammal" and the overlap $\mathrm{Vol}(A \cap B)/\mathrm{Vol}(B)$ reads as $P(A \mid B)$ (Vilnis et al., ACL 2018, to add), and Gaussian embeddings, where breadth is covariance [@vilnis2015word]. Containment is asymmetric; hyperbolic distance is not, so the two answer different questions ("is it inside" and "how general is it"), which is to be tested on one hierarchy.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/tangent_spaces_geodesics.qmd, section sec-shape-tree -->
## The Shape of a Tree {#sec-shape-tree}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: what a representation is invariant to, how a static thing is a point and an event a curve, and where negative curvature helps: trees embed with low distortion in few dimensions, against the dimension cost of flat space. Achieved for the representation of meaning: meaning that survives symmetries (@sec-prop-invariance) and moves along paths (@sec-prop-paths), and hierarchies that fit as regions. Computation: some symmetries are absorbed by data and augmentation, and some survive because they are cheap, as convolution and rotary position embeddings did; whether hyperbolic geometry earns its cost beyond trees is read from its cost per step and its gain at matched dimension and compute, dated. Evidence at scale: for hyperbolic space, the authors' own results only; for rotary position embeddings, adoption at scale shows that they are cheap and does not show that they are better than learned positions, and an ablation is to be found (from memory, unchecked: the RoFormer paper). Smoke test: embed a small balanced tree in the plane and in a Poincaré disc, and compare the distortion of the tree distances, which has an analytic answer for the tree. Still out of reach: a hierarchy of definitions in which one idea has several parents is a graph and not a tree, so hyperbolic space holds the tree part only. Relations are the next step (@sec-ch-meaning-as-difference).*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/contextual_vectors.qmd, section sec-tree-geometry -->
## Is the Tree in the Geometry? {#sec-tree-geometry}
*Chomsky's phrase-structure trees, looked for inside trained models: subject-verb agreement across intervening clauses (2016), agreement in nonsense sentences, "colorless green" networks (2018), and the structural probe (2019), which finds parse-tree distance as squared distance in a linear subspace of BERT and tree depth as a squared norm. Against it, the theoretical limits of self-attention on unbounded bracket nesting and the positive result for bounded depth. Brackets are the right test because of the Chomsky–Schützenberger theorem (1963): every context-free language is built from balanced brackets (a Dyck language) and a regular language. Bounded depth is Chomsky's competence versus performance (1963–1965): people also parse only a few levels of centre-embedding, and a network with finite precision and context is, strictly, a large finite automaton.*

## Technologies That Exploit Regions {#sec-reg-technologies}
*Plan (about 1 page). Box and order embeddings for entailment and hypernymy, hyperbolic embeddings for taxonomies, Gaussian embeddings for breadth and ambiguity, and subspace models in the style of quantum-inspired semantics. For each: what it costs against a point of the same size, and whether the gain holds at matched tuning and scale; a shape that does not beat a point on its judge is dropped to `notes/ideas.qmd` with the check that failed it.*

## A Concept Has an Extent {#sec-reg-closing}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: whether typicality is recoverable from a centroid, whether categories are convex or held by chains, which shape of region carries hierarchy at low distortion and at what cost, and whether negation as complement works. Achieved for the representation of meaning: meanings as regions (@sec-prop-region), with the shapes that survive. Computation: whether curved spaces and boxes train as cheaply as flat ones. Still out of reach: a region is static, and an event changes (@sec-ch-meaning-as-generation).*

*Sources and gaps (first pass).* Sourced in `references/`: Rosch, Gärdenfors, Wittgenstein, Goodman, Putnam, the logic of subspaces, hyperbolic embeddings, boxes, the structural probe. Not yet read for this chapter: a typicality norm other than Rosch's own; the claim that a tree embeds with low distortion in a hyperbolic space of few dimensions is stated from the papers' own results and is to be checked by the toy run.

## Meaning Can Be a Region {#sec-prop-region}
*A concept is not always a point: it can be an area, a cone, or a subspace, and one concept can contain another.*

Figure (planned): "dog" as a region inside "animal", with the individual dogs as points within it.

Earned in this chapter (hierarchies in curved space, and concepts as subspaces).

Sources (first pass). Concepts as convex regions of a conceptual space [@gardenfors2000conceptual]; words as Gaussian densities instead of points [@vilnis2015word]; hierarchies embedded in hyperbolic space [@nickel2017poincare]; a parse tree recovered from distances under a linear map [@hewitt2019structural]; concepts as subspaces with a logic of their own [@widdows2004geometry; @birkhoff1936logic].

Sceptics and balance. None of the sceptical sources collected so far bears on this property, and the section says so instead of implying agreement: it rests on the sources above, has no counter-evidence gathered, and stays a hypothesis until a test is chosen.

<!-- salvaged from chapters/curse_of_dimensionality.qmd (snapshot: embedding-technologies-stubs-v2/curse_of_dimensionality.qmd), section sec-statistical-curse-why-learning -->

## The Statistical Curse: Why Learning Needs Structure {#sec-statistical-curse-why-learning}
*Bellman's name for it [@bellman1961adaptive] was about computation and learning, not geometry. A neighbourhood that holds 1% of uniform data in ten dimensions spans 63% of every axis, most points lie closer to the boundary than to any other point, and the sample size needed for the same density grows exponentially, so 100 points in one dimension become $100^{10}$ in ten [@hastie2009elements]. Knowing only that a function is smooth (Lipschitz), learning it takes a number of samples exponential in the dimension [@bronstein2021geometric]. The ways out are assumptions about structure, and the book follows three: data of low intrinsic dimension (the Manifold Hypothesis, below), symmetry (@sec-prop-invariance), and abstraction into a few relevant variables [@bernardi2020geometry], which returns as composition (@sec-ch-meaning-and-structure).*

<!-- salvaged from chapters/curse_of_dimensionality.qmd (snapshot: embedding-technologies-stubs-v2/curse_of_dimensionality.qmd), section sec-manifold-hypothesis -->

## The Manifold Hypothesis {#sec-manifold-hypothesis}
*Why real-world data saves us from empty high-dimensional voids ($d_{\text{int}} \ll D_{\text{ambient}}$): images of an object that can only shift and rotate lie on a three-dimensional manifold, whatever the number of pixels [@bishop2024deep]. @sec-ch-meaning-as-arrangement tests the hypothesis with persistent homology [@chung2021neural].*

*One manifold or several? A single intrinsic dimension for a whole dataset is an idealisation. If the data are a union of pieces of different dimension and curvature (a stratified space), then a fixed radius means different things in different pieces: it covers a tight neighbourhood in a dense, low-dimensional piece and many unrelated points in a sparse, high-dimensional one, and distance concentration (@sec-concentration-measure) sets in earlier where the local dimension is higher. The estimate of local intrinsic dimension from the ratio of distances to the first two neighbours (Facco et al. 2017, to add) is the check, and a map of it over a trained space is the test; no result for embedding spaces is held in `references/`, so the claim is an idea until one is read. Consequence taken up elsewhere: a global similarity threshold has no fixed meaning (@sec-reading-nearness-correctly).*

## Questions Handed On From the Likeness Chapter {#sec-likeness-handed-to-meaning-as-region}

Gärdenfors (2000) places meanings as regions of a space of quality dimensions and not as points [@gardenfors2000conceptual]. The quality dimensions of colour are hue, saturation and brightness, and "red" is the region of that space of the shades that we call red, with the clearest red at its centre and orange at its edge, where a shade is more or less red. A point holds one shade, and a region holds the concept and says what is inside. This matches Wittgenstein's concept "not closed by a frontier" [@wittgenstein1953philosophical, §68] when there is no exact shade at which red stops, and a boundary can be drawn for a purpose, but the concept worked before it was drawn.

::: {.test #q-likeness-17}
**Q17. Is a meaning a point?** Does a concept have an extent that a single point cannot hold, and does a region beat a point of the same size on a stated judge?

*See* @sec-ch-meaning-as-region.
:::
